ai.definition: Recursive AI systems are a type of machine learning model that continuously learns from its own output to improve performance over time. This process involves feeding back the system's predictions into itself as input for further iterations.
ai.howItWorks: These systems use feedback loops where the output of one iteration serves as input for subsequent ones, allowing them to refine and optimize their algorithms through repeated cycles of prediction and correction. This iterative learning can lead to more accurate models over time compared to traditional batch training methods.
ai.problemSolved: Recursive AI addresses the limitations of static machine learning models by enabling continuous improvement in performance without human intervention. It is particularly useful for tasks where data is constantly evolving or where long-term accuracy is critical, such as drug discovery and materials science.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing and deploying software that can handle recursive training processes. This includes creating robust feedback mechanisms and ensuring the system can manage large datasets efficiently.
ai.buildProcess: The build process starts with defining a base model, then setting up an iterative framework where predictions are continuously fed back into the model for retraining. This requires careful design of the feedback loop to avoid issues like overfitting or instability in the learning process.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the computational resources needed for repeated training cycles and the expertise required to develop effective recursive models. Data storage and processing costs are also significant factors.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive, with increasing adoption expected as more industries recognize the benefits of continuous learning in complex problem-solving domains.
ai.regulation: Current regulatory frameworks for AI vary widely. Specific regulations related to recursive AI are still emerging, particularly concerning data privacy and algorithmic transparency.
ai.risks: Risks include potential instability in the learning process, difficulty in explaining model decisions due to its iterative nature, and challenges in ensuring fairness and avoiding biases that may compound over iterations.
ai.profitability: Profitability depends on the specific application. In fields like drug discovery where traditional methods are expensive or slow, recursive AI can provide significant cost savings and speed up development timelines.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments will likely focus on improving efficiency, reliability, and explainability of recursive models to make them more accessible and trustworthy for a broader range of applications.

glossary.def: A process where the output of an AI model is used as input for further iterations to improve its performance over time.
A mechanism in recursive AI systems that allows the system's predictions to be continuously fed back into itself for retraining and improvement.
A condition where a model learns the training data too well, including noise and outliers, leading to poor generalization on new data.

subsystems.name: Base model and training stack
subsystems.role: the large neural network(s) that do the reasoning and generation.

subsystems.name: Search and proposal layer
subsystems.role: generates candidate improvements — to code, architecture, hyperparameters, data or training recipe.

subsystems.name: Evaluation harness
subsystems.role: decides whether a proposed change is actually better, on held-out tasks.

subsystems.name: Sandboxed execution environment
subsystems.role: runs AI-written code safely and reproducibly.

subsystems.name: Self-improvement controller
subsystems.role: closes the loop: propose, test, keep the winners, retrain or rewrite.

subsystems.name: Oversight layer
subsystems.role: watches for the loop drifting into unsafe or degenerate behaviour.
parts: human approval gates and an off switch

subsystems.name: Domain simulators and data engines
subsystems.role: supply fast, cheap ground truth for science problems.

buildSteps.title: Train a strong base model
buildSteps.detail: Pretrain on text, code and scientific data so the system can read, write and reason about its own source.

buildSteps.title: Give it tools
buildSteps.detail: Attach a code interpreter, retrieval over documentation, and access to simulators so proposals can be executed rather than just described.

buildSteps.title: Define verifiable objectives
buildSteps.detail: Choose problems with automatic, objective scoring — a test suite that passes, a simulation result, a measured property — because an unmeasurable goal cannot drive a loop.

buildSteps.title: Add the search layer
buildSteps.detail: Wrap the model in a population-based search that proposes many candidate changes and scores each one, keeping the best.

buildSteps.title: Automate the cycle
buildSteps.detail: Replace human steps one at a time: generate, execute, evaluate, select, retrain. Each turn produces a recorded lineage of what changed and why.

buildSteps.title: Sandbox and checkpoint everything
buildSteps.detail: Every generation runs in an isolated environment with compute and time caps, and is snapshotted so a bad lineage can be rolled back.

buildSteps.title: Add capability and safety gates
buildSteps.detail: Before any self-modification is kept, run evaluations for loss of control, reward hacking and dangerous capabilities; require human sign-off for large jumps.

buildSteps.title: Scale iteratively
buildSteps.detail: Widen what the loop is allowed to change — first hyperparameters, then training code, then architecture, then its own search procedure — only as fast as verification can keep up.

prerequisites.why: the loop is only as good as the model proposing the changes.

prerequisites.tech: Automated machine learning and architecture search
prerequisites.why: already deployed for tuning models, and is the narrow ancestor of a self-improving loop.

prerequisites.tech: Trustworthy automatic evaluation of open-ended work
prerequisites.why: tests exist for code and maths, but 'is this research idea better?' still needs human judgement.
containers work, but containing a system that can rewrite itself is much harder than containing ordinary software.

prerequisites.tech: Interpretability and control of learned systems
prerequisites.why: without it, no one can tell whether a self-modification removed a safety property.
science domains need cheap, high-throughput experiments to give the loop a signal.

pathway.milestone: AI that assists AI work: code assistants, automated tuning, search that discovers better algorithms and chip layouts
pathway.unlocks: measurable speed-ups in narrow, verifiable engineering tasks.

pathway.milestone: agent systems that run whole experimental cycles in one domain, such as candidate molecules or battery materials, with humans reviewing results
pathway.unlocks: research throughput limited mainly by laboratory capacity rather than by people.

pathway.milestone: self-improvement loops approved on well-verifiable tasks end to end, under sandboxing and audit
pathway.unlocks: evidence about whether the loop compounds or stalls.

pathway.milestone: loops allowed to modify their own training and search code
pathway.unlocks: faster progress, but only if interpretability, evaluation and governance keep pace; compute, data and the cost of verification remain the binding limits.
